prompt: Which of these does a diagram written as text give that a drawing tool's file does not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of a pull request and a build.

choices.text: A diff a reviewer can read
choices.why: Yes: one new line per container or relationship, instead of a changed binary file.

choices.text: A check that fails when the diagram does not parse
choices.why: Yes: a renderer refuses a broken file, and a build can turn that into a red step.

choices.text: Full control over where each box is placed
choices.why: The opposite: the tool places the boxes, which is one of the costs.

choices.text: Generation from another source, such as configuration
choices.why: Yes: text can be written by a program, which keeps reference diagrams true.

prompt: What makes Structurizr a different kind of tool from Mermaid and PlantUML?
hint: How many times is the ticketing API written?

choices.text: It draws prettier diagrams
choices.why: Looks are not the difference; the model is.

choices.text: It runs in the browser instead of a terminal
choices.why: All three have command-line renderers; this course ran Structurizr from a container.

choices.text: One model, and views derived from it
choices.why: Right: an element written once cannot appear differently on two views.

choices.text: It supports UML and nothing else
choices.why: It is built around C4; PlantUML is the UML specialist.

prompt: Match each tool to what it runs on in this lesson's lab.
hint: A JavaScript renderer, a jar, a container image.

prompt: Why does the lesson warn against the online editors for a real company's diagrams?

choices.text: They render more slowly than a local install
choices.why: Speed is not the concern the lesson raises.

choices.text: What you type goes to another company's server
choices.why: Yes: an architecture of a real system should not be sent to a third party without agreement.

choices.text: They draw state diagrams badly
choices.why: They draw the same diagrams; the issue is where the content goes.

choices.text: They require a paid account
choices.why: The lesson does not say so; it says their terms can change.

prompt: The browser mmdc downloads takes about 700 MB, PlantUML 30 MB and the Structurizr image about 730 MB. Roughly how many megabytes does the full installed path use?
Match each symptom to its likely cause.

pairs.right: the browser download was skipped or done as another user

pairs.left: docker: permission denied on the socket
pairs.right: the user may not talk to Docker
Node.js missing, or not on the PATH

right_distractors: the diagram has a syntax error

prompt: A diagram that rendered last month fails today, and nobody changed the file. What does the lesson say to check first?
hint: Every command in the lesson names something exact.

choices.text: Whether a tool's version changed
choices.why: Right: that is why every install and the pipeline pin a version.

choices.text: Whether the file has Windows line endings
choices.why: Possible, and not the first suspect when the file itself did not change.

choices.text: Whether the disk is full
choices.why: That breaks installs; it rarely turns a parse into a failure.

choices.text: Whether the diagram has too many elements
choices.why: Size does not stop a file that parsed last month.

prompt: In a Mermaid state diagram, the initial pseudostate is written as ___.
When broken.mmd fails to render, what does the lesson call the whole case for diagrams as text?

choices.text: The error message names the line
choices.why: Helpful, and still not the case the lesson makes.

choices.text: Mermaid draws faster than a person
choices.why: Speed is not the argument.

choices.text: The refusal: a machine catches the wrong diagram
choices.why: Yes: a drawing cannot be wrong in a way a machine notices; this one can, with a non-zero exit.

choices.text: GitHub shows the error in the pull request
choices.why: GitHub draws Mermaid; the check comes from running mmdc in the pipeline.

prompt: After rendering broken.mmd, the transcript echoes the exit status. What number did it print?
Match each PlantUML arrow to what it draws in a sequence diagram.
Why was the full purchase rendered as SVG rather than as text with -tutxt?
hint: What does the text renderer draw poorly?

choices.text: The text renderer needs Graphviz
choices.why: It needs nothing extra; it drew hold.puml in the terminal.

choices.text: It handles alt fragments poorly
choices.why: Right: plain messages render well as text; fragments do not.

choices.text: SVG files are smaller
choices.why: Size was not the reason given.

choices.text: Terminals display box-drawing characters badly
choices.why: The hold.puml transcript shows they can.

prompt: The pipeline script uses -checkonly rather than -syntax for PlantUML files. Why, by the lesson?

choices.text: -syntax is slower on large files
choices.why: Speed was not the reason.

choices.text: -checkonly also writes an image to inspect
choices.why: It checks without producing the image.

choices.text: -checkonly is stricter
choices.why: Yes: it also refuses a file with no complete diagram in it.

choices.text: -syntax was removed in this PlantUML version
choices.why: The transcript runs -syntax with this version.

prompt: What did the grep on the two exported files show about the relationship to the payment gateway?

choices.text: It appears on the container view alone
choices.why: The context view has it too, as the ticketing system's relationship.

choices.text: Written once, it is on both views
choices.why: Right: one model, so the two views cannot disagree about it.

choices.text: It is missing from the context view by mistake
choices.why: The count was 1 in both files.

choices.text: It appears twice on each view
choices.why: The count was 1 per file.

prompt: Which details of the docker run command does the lesson say matter? Choose all that apply.
hint: Who owns the output, and where it goes.

choices.text: --user, so the exported files are yours
choices.why: Yes: otherwise they belong to the container's user, or the export fails.

choices.text: Creating the output folder first
choices.why: Yes: the export fails when the folder does not exist.

choices.text: The image tag pinned to a date
choices.why: Yes: the same version every time.

choices.text: Running the container as root
choices.why: The opposite: the lesson passes your own user.

prompt: In the DSL's views block, include ___ lets the tool decide which elements belong in each view.
Put the pipeline step for diagrams in order.
items: Exit 1 if any failed, so the merge is blocked
trap: Checking before installing the pinned versions tests whatever happens to be on the runner.

prompt: For Structurizr, what deeper check than parsing does the lesson suggest in the pipeline?

choices.text: validate, which checks the model itself
choices.why: Right: relationships to elements that do not exist, duplicate names.

choices.text: Rendering each view to PNG
choices.why: Rendering proves it draws, not that the model is consistent.

choices.text: Comparing the exported files with last week's
choices.why: Change is not an error; the model's consistency is the check.

choices.text: A human review of each view
choices.why: Useful, and not what a pipeline step can do.

prompt: Match each need to the tool Carcará settled on.
hint: README, exact UML, agreeing views, the board.

pairs.left: a flow next to a service's code
a sequence diagram in a decision record
context and container views that agree

prompt: A colleague wants every diagram, including the board's slides, written in Structurizr. What does the lesson say?
hint: Who reads it, and what question does it answer?

choices.text: Agree: one tool is simpler
choices.why: Simpler for the authors, and a worse picture where layout is the message.

choices.text: Agree, but export to PNG
choices.why: The export format does not give back the deliberate layout a persuasive slide needs.

choices.text: Use text where it is reviewed; hand-draw what persuades
choices.why: Yes: a slide for one meeting is better drawn by hand and not kept.

choices.text: Refuse: Structurizr is for developers
choices.why: Its views serve many readers; the issue is layout for persuasion.
